issues.legal_issue: A statutory assistant charity commissioner exercising predominantly adjudicatory functions is a court for purposes of contempt law.
material_facts: Contempt proceedings followed a referral by the Assistant Charity Commissioner concerning newspaper publications said to interfere with the administration of justice.
The appeal challenged the High Court’s rejection of a preliminary objection that the Assistant Charity Commissioner was not a court.
The Assistant Charity Commissioner was a serving judicial officer whose services had been placed at the disposal of the government for appointment to the post.

The statutory officer inquired into whether a trust existed, whether it was a public trust, and whether property belonged to it, and could hear parties, receive evidence, and decide those questions by applying the law.
The officer had powers to summon and examine witnesses on oath, compel production of documents, and use other specified civil-procedure powers in inquiries.
The officer’s decisions were final and conclusive unless set aside through the statutory avenues of review or appeal, and civil-court jurisdiction over matters assigned to the officer was barred.
The officer’s functions were predominantly adjudicatory, although the officer also performed administrative functions.
issues.conclusion: The Assistant Charity Commissioner possessed the attributes of a court and was a court for purposes of Sections 2 and 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a statutory authority is a court depends on the statute’s scheme and whether the authority has the attributes of a court: it must decide disputes judicially, hear parties and consider evidence, and be empowered to give a definitive, authoritative judgment with finality. The Court applied Sections 5, 18, 19, 70, 72–80 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950, as applicable to Karnataka, including its provisions on inquiries, procedural powers, judicial proceedings, finality, appeals, and exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction. It also considered the approach in The Bharat Bank Ltd. v. Employees of the Bharat Bank Ltd. (1950) SCR 459; Brajnandan Sinha v. Jyoti Narain (1955) 2 SCR 955; Shri Virindar Kumar Satyawadi v. The State of Punjab (1955) 2 SCR 1013; and Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. (1967) 3 SCR 163.

predicates.proceeding_is_appeal_from_preliminary_ru: The proceeding is an appeal from a preliminary ruling in contempt proceedings about whether a statutory officer is a court.
predicates.statutory_officer_has_legal_judicial_qua: The statute requires the officer to have a judicial or legal background.
predicates.officer_decides_disputes_after_hearing_p: The officer hears the parties, considers evidence, and applies the law to decide disputes.
predicates.officer_can_compel_attendance_and_produc: The officer can require people to attend and give evidence and can compel production of documents.
predicates.officer_gives_definitive_authoritative_d: The officer gives definitive decisions that carry authority and finality unless altered through an available appeal or review.
predicates.civil_court_jurisdiction_is_excluded_for: Civil courts cannot decide disputes that the statutory scheme assigns to the officer and makes final through its prescribed process.
predicates.officer_functions_are_predominantly_adju: The officer’s principal functions involve deciding disputes rather than performing administrative tasks.

issues.definition: When the proceeding is an appeal from a preliminary ruling in contempt proceedings and the statutory officer has the stated qualifications, adjudicatory powers, decision-making authority, and predominantly adjudicatory role, the officer is treated as a court for contempt purposes.
